GJT.name: Grand Junction
GJT.excerpt: High pressure will be positioned to the southeast over Texas with the low off the SoCal coast, allowing deeper moisture to advect northward through southeast Utah and southwest Colorado Wednesday through Thursday.
GJT.text:
CONTINUED COOL THIS WEEKEND WITH WARMUP INTO EARLY THIS WEEK:

Clouds are beginning to increase from the southwest this evening as the high pressure shifts eastward allowing some moisture to work in the southwest flow. A weak shortwave disturbance will track through the Four Corners Sunday allowing for some isolated light showers to form over the San Juans. This continues into Monday with better coverage of showers across the central and southern mountains. Very little in the way of forcing will lend itself to light precipitation amounts with a dusting of snow possible above treeline in the San Juans. Temperatures will near normal Sunday with a bit of WAA heading into Tuesday and Wednesday ahead of a deep closed low that will dive down the west coast and close off over SoCal.

High pressure will be positioned to the southeast over Texas with the low off the SoCal coast, allowing deeper moisture to advect northward through southeast Utah and southwest Colorado Wednesday through Thursday. PWAT anomalies climb towards 300 percent of normal during this time, which equates to PWAT of 0.75 to 1 inch across much of the area with PWAT above an inch over the Four Corners. Showers become more widespread Wednesday and Thursday in this moist southwest flow with potential for more substantial rainfall for southern Colorado and southeast Utah. There is also potential for mountain snowfall but it all depends on how much cold air arrives with this low pressure system. Models have not been in great agreement on the depth of cold air and seem to be trending milder as this low lifts across the Great Basin and into the northern Rockies Thursday night into Friday, with the coldest air now across Montana and Wyoming. Much cooler temperatures arrive on the backside of this low Friday into the coming weekend with unsettled conditions in the northwest flow through next Saturday for the mountains. BOU.name: Boulder / Denver
BOU.excerpt: As we approach next weekend, guidance generally tries to push cooler air into the plains.
BOU.text:
The forecast hasn't changed much in the last day. We continue to sit underneath a broad ridge, while a weak cutoff low spins over far southern California. Water vapor satellite shows plenty of dry air over the forecast area, and unsurprisingly there hasn't been much (if any) cloud cover over the last 24 hours.

Sunday will be another very quiet day for the region, with temperatures a few degrees cooler than Saturday. A gradual increase in mid/high cloud cover is expected during the day as that weak cutoff low begins drifting to the northeast and upper level moisture slowly starts working into the state.

That upper low should shear out into an open wave as it continues to drift towards the area on Monday. There should be more cloud cover during the day, and mid-level temperatures will be a couple degrees cooler, leading to forecast highs in the upper 60s to low 70s Monday afternoon. A few light rain or snow showers will be possible across the higher elevations but little to no accumulation is anticipated.

A stronger closed 500mb low is expected to approach the California coast mid-week, with strengthening south-southwesterly flow aloft. Moisture will slowly increase from mid to late week as that low works eastward into the intermountain west. Chances for rain and snow showers over the higher elevations return to the forecast by Wednesday night, with more coverage expected by Thursday or Friday. Generally light precipitation amounts are expected across our forecast area, with more significant rain/snow accumulation over southwestern Colorado.

As we approach next weekend, guidance generally tries to push cooler air into the plains. Ensemble guidance is split 50/50 on whether the I-25 corridor manages any precipitation, but at the very least this should get high temperatures back closer to normal values for mid/late October (low 60s).

PUB.name: Pueblo
PUB.excerpt: Saturday and Sunday...uncertainty increases for next weekend with the evolution of the upper pattern. NBM pop grids look good, with low end precipitation chances across the area on Saturday, drying out for the weekend.
PUB.text:
Not much change to the extended forecast, with good agreement through the end of the week, and differences arising by next weekend with the upper pattern. Very wet conditions are still favored along the Continental Divide, focused on the San Juan Range.

Monday through Tuesday...persistent southwest flow will prevail across Colorado through the early part of the work week. Weak embedded energy will keep persistent shower activity going along the Continental Divide through much of this period. At this time, all shower activity looks to remain west, where the main energy lifts across western Colorado, to the northeast. Very weak instability could lead to a couple rumbles of thunder Monday and Tuesday afternoons. Snow levels will be high, above 13 kft, and a dusting of snow may be possible at best. Across the Plains, a weak cold front will arrive by Monday morning, which will help keep temperatures cool, mainly in the 60s. Temperatures will once again warm up on Tuesday, with mostly 70s for the lower elevations.

Wednesday through Friday...models still bringing a strong storm system across the region for mid to late week. There remains differences in storm track, with the ECMWF furthest south, and the GFS/Canadian north. All guidance and ensembles have a deep moisture tap off the eastern Pacific, and PWAT values will climb to near an inch across the region. Showers will increase in coverage along the Continental Divide on Wednesday, peaking in intensity Wednesday night into Thursday, and likely linger across the region into Friday. NBM guidance, ensembles and deterministic guidance all have 1 to 3 inches of QPF across the San Juan Range during this period. NBM is centered around 3 inches, and WPC guidance is in excess of 4 for the days 5-7 period. DESI probs of 2 inches or more are greater than 50% for the San Juan Range. CYS.name: Cheyenne
CYS.excerpt: The upper level low will make its exit to the east sometime in the Friday through Sunday period. This will present the next chance for notable precipitation, while also dropping temperatures closer to seasonal normals.
CYS.text:
Warm and dry weather is expected to continue through most of next week, though a transition to a more active pattern is possible by the end of the week into next weekend. The synoptic weather pattern for the weak ahead will features a broad ridge over the central US, with another slow moving closed low meandering into the western part of the country. Southwest flow aloft will prevail through most of the week. Temperatures will be well above seasonal averages with 700- mb temperatures around +5 to +8C for much of the week. Look for highs in the mid 60s to mid 70s across the area, which will be about 10-15F above normal. The flow direction will continue to improve mid to upper level moisture through the week. By Thursday afternoon, NAEFS mean precipitable water is actually quite close to climatological maximums. Despite the high moisture content, we don't have much lift to actually translate this into precipitation. Weak heating this late in the season will keep convective instability to a minimum, and synoptic forcing appears unimpressive at this time. Still, we may see some widely scattered high-based showers each afternoon and early evening through the week ahead. Forcing may be strong enough by Thursday to pick up coverage a little as the upper level low to our west inches closer. Fortunately, the moisture advection will mix into the boundary layer periodically, which should keep fire weather concerns down.

The upper level low will make its exit to the east sometime in the Friday through Sunday period. This will present the next chance for notable precipitation, while also dropping temperatures closer to seasonal normals. Most likely, Friday will be another warm day but with increasing chances for rainfall later in the day, with the cool- down waiting until Saturday. Since we are still 6 to 7 days out, precipitation is highly uncertain at this time. NBM PoPs are generally in the 30 to 50% range which seems appropriate at this lead time. SLC.name: Salt Lake City
SLC.excerpt: - Modest snow accumulation of around 3" to 6" will be possible above 9500 ft or so as snow levels dip Thursday into late Friday.
SLC.text:
- Isolated showers and thunderstorms return to southern and central Utah Sunday and Monday.

- Widespread precipitation chances return as early as Tuesday and continue on through Friday. Forecast water amounts are around 0.50" to 1.50", with locally up to 2.00" or so in favored high terrain.

- Modest snow accumulation of around 3" to 6" will be possible above 9500 ft or so as snow levels dip Thursday into late Friday.

BOI.name: Boise
BOI.excerpt: The upper-level low pressure system will slowly move inland into the Great Basin Wednesday and Thursday. At the same time, another upper-level trough will approach the BC, Canada coast.
BOI.text: The upper-level low pressure system will slowly move inland into the Great Basin Wednesday and Thursday. At the same time, another upper-level trough will approach the BC, Canada coast. Ensembles have the closed low in the Great Basin rejoining the flow and moving east of the area Friday and Saturday. Most areas see a chance of precipitation during this period, though the track of the low continues to favor SW Idaho zones with the greatest coverage and amounts. The heaviest rainfall totals remain focused over w-central Idaho, with widespread 0.25-0.50 inch amounts and locally up to 0.75 inches for Thur/Fri. Thunderstorm chances also accompany the precipitation chances, with the greatest coverage and percentage chances happening on Thursday. Snow levels will drop from 9-10kft MSL Wed/Thur to 6-8kft MSL on Friday as the wrap around precipitation ends. Additionally, late Thursday into Friday, a significant cold front is expected to move through the area. Winds through the western Snake Plain are expected to be 20-30 mph Friday afternoon as that moves through the area. Temperatures are forecast to be near- or just below-normal Friday through Sunday, with another significant upper-level trough looking to impact the area Sunday.
